rounds.proof_sketch: The optimized kernel is launched with grid_size.y = N = 4096. Therefore blockIdx.y ∈ [0, N-1] = [0, 4095], which means row = blockIdx.y ∈ [0, 4095]. The original condition 'row < N' evaluates to 'row < 4096', which is always true for row ∈ [0, 4095]. The mutated condition 'row <= N' evaluates to 'row <= 4096', which is also always true for row ∈ [0, 4095]. Both conditions are always true—the boundary case row == N is unreachable.
rounds.survival_reason: The grid launch configuration directly ties grid_size.y to N, meaning blockIdx.y (and hence the row variable in the kernel) can only take values from 0 to N-1. The mutation changes 'row < N' to 'row <= N', which would only differ when row == N. However, since the CUDA grid dimension ensures row never equals N, both conditions always evaluate identically to true. The mutation cannot produce any observable difference regardless of input tensor values because the distinguishing case (row == N) is architecturally unreachable given the fixed launch parameters.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The grid launch with grid_size.y = N ensures blockIdx.y ranges [0, N-1], making row always strictly less than N. The mutation from '<' to '<=' has no effect since row == N never occurs. No value-level test can expose the difference because the boundary is determined by launch configuration, not input values.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing of CUDA boundary conditions, trace thread/block indices through grid launch configurations to their concrete ranges. Mutations affecting predicates like 'row < N' can be equivalent if grid dimensions enforce row < N structurally. Consider launch configuration mutations (e.g., grid_size.y = N+1) as separate mutation targets to expose such boundary guard logic.
